newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka stock crackdown seen yielding positive results.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka stock crackdown seen yielding positive results.

text.p: The long-term impact of a court-ordered crackdown on share price manipulators, which has included arrest warrants for the stock exchange chairman and 35 others, should be positive, brokers said on Thursday.

"There has been an initial shock in the market in the wake of the crackdown. But I am sure about its positive impact in the market in the long run," broker Abdul Rashid, owner of his own broking firm, told Reuters.
A Bangladeshi court has ordered the arrest of 36 brokers and company owners on charges of manipulating share prices, police said on Thursday.

The arrest warrants, including those for DSE chairman Imtiyaz Husain and renowned industrialist Salman Rahman, were issued by the chief metropolitan magistrate on Wednesday night, but police said they had not yet been able to detain any of the suspects.
Under SEC rules offenders can be imprisoned for up to five years or fined 500,000 taka ($11,548).
"We launched an immediate search last night but no one was found at their homes," one police officer said.
Police said the news of arrest warrents apparently reached the suspects before police arrived.
"Big guys have many (information) channels and their own intelligence network," one police officer said. Others said the suspects were likely to surrender to the court and apply for bail.

Police said the arrest orders were issued after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the watchdog of the country's capital market, filed cases against the suspects for alleged "fraudulent activities" in the capital market.
The cases were filed at the court of the chief metropolitan magistrate on the basis of a report from a four-member inquiry committee headed by Professor Aminul Islam Chowdhury.
The committee was formed on December 26 after stock prices began falling sharply in the wake of a four-month rally, triggering turmoil in the capital market.
Rashid said there was little reason to panic following the legal issuance of arrest orders. "I am confident that this will restore the confidence of the investors," he said.
Rashid hailed the government's move, saying that "it had set a very good example. The market will now stabilise and (it will signal) that there will be no manipulation in the future."
Brokers said the action did not even spare the son-in-law of the SEC chairman Haroonur Rashid, Anu Jaigirdar, an owner of Premium Securities Ltd.
Jaigirdar was also on the arrest list, police said.
The SEC chairman said the move would restore confidence in the capital market.
"The government is determined to root out corruption and irregularities in the securities market," he told Reuters.
Redwanul Islam, a trader with Dastagir M. Adil & Co., said he hoped for a positive impact from the government steps.
"Let us hope for the best. The market may stabilise soon. We expect a better result from this new experience," he said.
Share prices on the DSE were falling on Thursday as most mahajor investors stayed away following news of the arrest warrants.
"Those trading are also somewhat nervous," one broker said.
The DSE benchmark index was at 1,225.49 on Wednesday, compared with 3,600 in the first week of October.
The stock market started its steep climb soon after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina took power following an election in June 1996.
The DSE index was below 1,000 at the time of the election but rallied afterwards as thousands of people, encouraged by the prospect of political stability, began trading in an unofficial kerb market.
In November, the SEC imposed circuit breakers on price movements to stabilise the market and warned against trading in 24 companies with poor financial track records.
